t: Maximum Good Subarray Sum — Prefix Sums + Hash Map
o: We need the maximum-sum subarray whose first and last **values** differ by exactly `k`. Values can repeat anywhere, so we cannot just scan neighbors. Using prefix sums, the sum of `nums[i..j]` is `P[j] - P[i-1]`; to maximize it for a fixed `j`, we want the **minimum** prefix `P[i-1]` among earlier positions `i` with `nums[i] = nums[j] ± k`. In example 2 (`[-1,3,2,4,5], k=3`), at `j=4` (value 5) we look for earlier 2's; position 2 has value 2 with prefix 4, giving `15-4=11`. Since `|nums[i]| ≤ 1e9` and `n ≤ 1e5`, sums reach ~1e14, so 64-bit integers are required.
k: Sum(i..j) = P[j] - P[i-1]; maximize by keeping the minimum prefix per value.

a.n: Approach 1: One-pass hash map of minimum prefixes
a.i: Sweep left to right maintaining `best[v]` = smallest prefix sum seen at positions holding value `v`. Before inserting the current position, query `best[nums[j]-k]` and `best[nums[j]+k]`; any hit yields a good subarray ending at `j`. Inserting after querying guarantees `i < j`.
s: Maintain running prefix `p` and map value → min prefix seen so far.
For each element, try both `x-k` and `x+k` in the map and update the answer with `p - stored`.
Then relax `best[x]` with the current prefix `p`.
Return the answer, or 0 if no good subarray was found.
a.t: O(n) — single pass with O(1) average hash operations
a.sp: O(n) — hash map stores at most n values

w: The key pitfall is overflow (use 64-bit sums) and negative numbers (never clamp the answer at 0 during the sweep — only at the end). A common follow-up asks for the maximum-sum subarray with difference *at most* k, which needs a balanced BST / sorted container instead of a hash map.
